summary.en: Designed toward future CME accreditation, this post-graduate clinical course prepares aesthetic and dermatologic clinicians to appraise the endocrine physiology of skin, differentiate pathognomonic endocrine cutaneous signs from isolated cosmetic presentations, evaluate the GRADE evidence and pharmacodynamics of cutaneous peptides and incretin therapies, and navigate regulatory and liability boundaries without promoting unapproved dosing protocols or commercial bias.

other licensed providers (pharmacists, naturopathic doctors, allied aesthetic professionals) who advise on skin products and referrals

professionalScope.en: Continuing professional education for licensed clinicians and allied providers. Every learner gets the same evidence, regulatory status and safety content; what each may do with it — prescribe, recommend, administer, or refer — follows their own licence and scope, and the course adapts its practice guidance to that role. It informs clinical reasoning; it is not a protocol, contains no dosing, and does not replace specialist input, formal guidelines or individual judgment.

disclaimers.en: Educational content for clinicians. It does not prescribe, and it never restates an evidence grade above what the source assigns to the specific indication.
Regulatory statements name their jurisdiction. US compounding examples (FDA 503A/503B) do not describe UK or EU status.
Designed toward future CME accreditation. No CME or CE credit is currently offered.

citations.title: Neuro-immuno-endocrinology of the skin: how environment regulates body homeostasis
citations.authors: Slominski RM, Raman C, Jetten AM, Slominski AT

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 1 — the four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) and the three routes (local, neural, circulation) · PMID 40263492 · Publisher correction PMID 40316721. Guide reference resolves exactly.

citations.title: Neuroendocrinology of the skin
citations.authors: Slominski A, Wortsman J

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 3, ch.6 ref 3, ch.7 ref 4 — CRH, POMC, ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin are made in skin with their receptors (para/autocrine action); dermal and epidermal units · PMID 11041445 · Erratum 2002. Also cited by A&RE ch.7 for the estrogen–senescence statement, which this 2000 review does not address (see findings).

citations.title: The human skin as a hormone target and an endocrine gland
citations.authors: Zouboulis CC

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 4, ch.7 ref 2 — skin makes, activates and releases hormones, including sex steroids that matter for the whole organism, especially in older people · PMID 16982574 · Verified; no PMCID.

citations.title: Neuronal control of skin function: the skin as a neuroimmunoendocrine organ
citations.authors: Roosterman D, Goerge T, Schneider SW, Bunnett NW, Steinhoff M

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 13 — sensory nerves and neuropeptides as the neural arm of the skin's signalling network · PMID 17015491 · Verified.

citations.title: Steroidogenesis in the skin: implications for local immune functions
citations.authors: Slominski A, Zbytek B, Nikolakis G, et al.

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 4 — skin cells hold the full apparatus (CYP11A1 onward) to make glucocorticoids, androgens and estrogens or activate circulating precursors; the review also describes a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens · PMID 23435015 · Verified.

citations.title: Keratinocytes control skin immune homeostasis through de novo-synthesized glucocorticoids
citations.authors: Phan TS, Schink L, Mann J, et al.

note.en: mouse genetic model (keratinocyte Cyp11b1 deletion) plus human disease association · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 5 — keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids restrain skin inflammation; the functional proof is in mice · PMID 33514551 · The guide presents this without naming the species; the course labels it as animal evidence.

citations.title: Human hair follicles display a functional equivalent of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and synthesize cortisol
citations.authors: Ito N, Ito T, Kromminga A, et al.

note.en: human scalp hair follicles in organ culture (ex vivo) · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 11 — CRH → POMC/ACTH → cortisol secretion with glucocorticoid feedback on CRH, in follicles with no systemic connections · PMID 15946990 · Verified.

citations.title: Human Hair Follicles Operate a Functional Peripheral Equivalent of the Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Somatotropic Axis Ex Vivo
citations.authors: Horesh EJ, Gherardini J, Alam M, et al.

note.en: research letter; human follicles ex vivo · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 12 — a GH/IGF-1 loop in the follicle · PMID 36496194 · No abstract indexed and not open access; cited only for the finding its title states.

citations.title: Thyroid hormone action in epidermal development and homeostasis and its implications in the pathophysiology of the skin
citations.authors: Mancino G, Miro C, Di Cicco E, Dentice M

note.en: narrative review (mouse models of thyroid-hormone metabolism) · academic · role: A&RE ch.6 ref 7 — local deiodinase control of T3 in keratinocytes; the review says the mechanisms are being clarified mainly in mouse models · PMID 33683663 · Verified.

citations.title: Photosynthesis of previtamin D3 in human skin and the physiologic consequences
citations.authors: Holick MF, MacLaughlin JA, Clark MB, et al.

note.en: human skin photobiology · academic · role: the skin-to-body example: previtamin D3 forms in human skin under solar UV and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation by vitamin D-binding protein · PMID 6251551 · Not cited by either guide; added as the primary for the statement that skin supplies a whole-body hormone system.

citations.title: Vitamin D metabolism, mechanism of action, and clinical applications
citations.authors: Bikle DD

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 3 — vitamin D3 made in skin from 7-dehydrocholesterol, then 25(OH)D and 1,25(OH)2D elsewhere · PMID 24529992 · Verified.

citations.title: Thyroid hormone action on skin
citations.authors: Safer JD

note.en: clinical review · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 8 — the skin signs of thyroid disease (myxoedema; dry, coarse skin) · PMID 22110782 · Verified (a 2012 review with the same title exists, PMID 22914563; the guide's volume and pages match this one).

citations.title: A Hormone Cell Atlas maps the human endocrine system at cellular resolution
citations.authors: Fei L, Huang-Doran I, Lawler K, et al. (senior authors Teichmann SA, Farooqi IS)

note.en: single-cell and single-nucleus transcriptomic atlas (hormone2cell): 379 hormone and receptor genes, ~14 million cells and nuclei, 47 human tissues · academic (University of Cambridge, Wellcome Sanger Institute) · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 1 — predicted hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types; the transcriptomic map the lesson is about · PMID 42207862 · PubMed entry 2026-05-28 (the guide's 'published online May 28, 2026'); print issue 2 Jul 2026. Full text and supplement paywalled (HTTP 403); only abstract- and portal-level facts are taught.

citations.title: Hormone Cell Atlas portal — About and FAQs
citations.authors: Hormone Cell Atlas team (Farooqi and Teichmann groups)

note.en: data portal · atlas authors · role: the authors' own usage statement: predictions are 'putative and hypothesis-generating, rather than … functional hormones and receptors', validation is the user's responsibility; 47 disease-free tissues, 1,900+ cell types, 14 million+ cells; skin is listed among the tissues on the sister cellxgene site (hormonecellatlas.cellgeni.sanger.ac.uk) · Fetched live 2026-09-24 (HTTP 200).

citations.title: On the Dependency of Cellular Protein Levels on mRNA Abundance
citations.authors: Liu Y, Beyer A, Aebersold R

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: transcript levels by themselves are not sufficient to predict protein levels in many scenarios · PMID 27104977 · Not cited by either guide; added to support the RNA-versus-protein step.

citations.title: The effect of sunscreen on vitamin D: a review
citations.authors: Neale RE, Khan SR, Lucas RM, Waterhouse M, Whiteman DC, Olsen CM

note.en: systematic review (MOOSE): 4 experimental studies, 3 field trials (2 RCTs), 69 observational studies · academic (QIMR Berghofer, Australian National University) · role: tests the guide's pearl that serum 25(OH)D falls with sunscreen use: experiments with artificial UV show a block; randomized field trials of daily sunscreen (SPF ~16) show no fall; high-SPF products untested · PMID 30945275 · Not cited by either guide; contradicts A&RE ch.7 testing pearl (see findings).

citations.title: Senescence-associated secretory phenotypes reveal cell-nonautonomous functions of oncogenic RAS and the p53 tumor suppressor
citations.authors: Coppé JP, Patil CK, Rodier F, et al.

note.en: cultured human fibroblasts and epithelial cells after genotoxic stress (+ prostate tumours after chemotherapy) · academic · role: defines the SASP (IL-6, IL-8 and other secreted factors) — the concept the guide uses · PMID 19053174 · Not cited by either guide; the primary behind 'SASP'.

citations.title: p16INK4A is a robust in vivo biomarker of cellular aging in human skin
citations.authors: Ressler S, Bartkova J, Niederegger H, et al.

note.en: human skin tissue bank, cross-sectional (0–20, 21–70, 71–95 years) · academic · role: p16-positive cells are more numerous in older skin, in both epidermis and dermis · PMID 16911562 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: P16INK4a Positive Cells in Human Skin Are Indicative of Local Elastic Fiber Morphology, Facial Wrinkling, and Perceived Age
citations.authors: Waaijer ME, Gunn DA, Adams PD, et al.
citations.publication: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci · 2016;71:1022–1028

note.en: cohort (Leiden Longevity Study), n=178, aged 45–81, sun-protected upper-inner-arm biopsies · academic; one co-author from Unilever; NIH and Cancer Research UK grants · role: senescent-cell counts in human skin track with elastic-fibre changes, facial wrinkles and perceived age, independent of chronological age; lowest vs highest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked ~3 years younger · PMID 26286607 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Faces of cellular senescence in skin aging
citations.authors: Ho CY, Dreesen O

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 5 — senescent cells accumulate in several human skin compartments; cell types respond differently · PMID 34166688 · Verified.

citations.title: Biomarkers of Cellular Senescence and Skin Aging
citations.authors: Wang AS, Dreesen O

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.7 ref 6 — no universal biomarker identifies senescent cells unequivocally; markers by skin compartment · PMID 30190724 · Full text (PMC6115505) read: it does not discuss estrogen loss or hormone responsiveness, which A&RE ch.7 cites it for.

citations.title: Targeting cellular senescence in dermatology: senolytic and senomorphic strategies
citations.authors: Haykal D, Flament F, Garibyan L, Lee K, Escot J, Gueniche A, Kirkland J

note.en: narrative review (no new data) · three authors from L'Oréal and a senolytic-field investigator; declares no competing interests · role: how dermatologic senotherapy stands in 2026: a review of mechanism and prospects; transient senescence aids wound repair · PMID 42417965 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: The influence of age and sex on skin thickness, skin collagen and density
citations.authors: Shuster S, Black MM, McVitie E

note.en: cross-sectional reference measurements of forearm skin · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 1 — skin collagen falls with age and is lower in women at all ages · PMID 1220811 · The abstract gives no annual rate; the guide's '~1% per year' could not be checked and is not taught.

citations.title: Decreased collagen production in chronologically aged skin: roles of age-dependent alteration in fibroblast function and defective mechanical stimulation
citations.authors: Varani J, Dame MK, Rittie L, et al.

note.en: human skin sections (18–29 vs 80+ years) and isolated dermal fibroblasts · academic · role: aged fibroblasts make less procollagen and are less attached to and stretched by collagen — two routes to lower synthesis · PMID 16723701 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Collagen fragmentation promotes oxidative stress and elevates matrix metalloproteinase-1 in fibroblasts in aged human skin
citations.authors: Fisher GJ, Quan T, Purohit T, et al.

note.en: aged (>80) vs young (21–30) human skin in vivo, plus organ and collagen-lattice culture · academic · role: more fibroblast MMP-1 in aged human dermis; fragmented collagen lowers fibroblast stretch and raises MMP-1 and oxidants — a self-perpetuating loop · PMID 19116368 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Mechanisms of photoaging and chronological skin aging
citations.authors: Fisher GJ, Kang S, Varani J, et al.

note.en: narrative review with new data · academic · role: A&RE ch.5 ref 2 — UV drives the matrix breakdown of photoageing, and photoageing and chronological ageing share molecular pathways · PMID 12437452 · Verified.

citations.title: Naturally occurring p16(Ink4a)-positive cells shorten healthy lifespan
citations.authors: Baker DJ, Childs BG, Durik M, et al.

note.en: mouse (INK-ATTAC transgene) · academic · role: A&RE ch.13 ref 2 — clearing p16-positive cells from one year of age extended median lifespan and delayed kidney, heart and fat deterioration; skin was checked for safety only (thickness, fibrosis), and clearance during healing slowed wound closure (Extended Data Fig. 10) · PMID 26840489 · Verified.

citations.title: Senolytics improve physical function and increase lifespan in old age
citations.authors: Xu M, Pirtskhalava T, Farr JN, et al.

note.en: mouse, plus human adipose-tissue explants · several authors hold a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds senolytic patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 1 — senescent cells cause dysfunction when transplanted; senolytics improved function and post-treatment survival in old mice · PMID 29988130 · Verified.

citations.title: Senolytics decrease senescent cells in humans: Preliminary report from a clinical trial of Dasatinib plus Quercetin in individuals with diabetic kidney disease
citations.authors: Hickson LJ, Langhi Prata LGP, Bobart SA, et al.

note.en: open-label phase 1 pilot, n=9, diabetic kidney disease (NCT02848131) · investigators with a financial interest; Mayo Clinic holds patents · role: A&RE ch.17 ref 3 — after a short course, epidermal p16- and p21-positive cells and circulating SASP factors fell; tissue-marker endpoints only · PMID 31542391 · Corrigendum PMID 31982828. The course does not report doses.

citations.title: Topical rapamycin reduces markers of senescence and aging in human skin: an exploratory, prospective, randomized trial
citations.authors: Chung CL, Lawrence I, Hoffman M, et al.

note.en: exploratory placebo-controlled RCT; 36 enrolled, 19 discontinued or lost to follow-up (NCT03103893) · academic (Drexel University) · role: the one randomized study of a senomorphic in human skin found: p16 protein fell and collagen VII rose; clinical change described only in 'multiple participants' · PMID 31761958 · Not cited by either guide.

citations.title: Sunscreen and prevention of skin aging: a randomized trial
citations.authors: Hughes MC, Williams GM, Baker P, Green AC

note.en: community RCT (Nambour), n=903 adults under 55, 4.5 years, blinded assessors (ACTRN12610000086066) · public (National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia) · role: daily sunscreen: no detectable increase in skin ageing over 4.5 years and 24% less ageing than discretionary use · PMID 23732711 · Not cited by either guide (A&RE ch.10 recommends sun protection without a trial citation).

citations.title: Topical tretinoin for treating photoaging: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials
citations.authors: Sitohang IBS, Makes WI, Sandora N, Suryanegara J

note.en: systematic review of 7 RCTs · academic; no conflicts declared · role: the randomized-trial base behind the guide's GRADE A for topical retinoids in photoageing: consistent improvement in wrinkling, mottled pigmentation and lentigines · PMID 35620028 · A&RE gives no citation for its GRADE A; this review supplies one.

citations.title: Improvement of naturally aged skin with vitamin A (retinol)
citations.authors: Kafi R, Kwak HS, Schumacher WE, et al.

note.en: randomized double-blind vehicle-controlled arm comparison, n=36, mean age 87, 24 weeks · academic (NIH-supported) · role: retinol improved fine wrinkling of naturally aged skin; biopsy subgroups showed more glycosaminoglycan and procollagen I · PMID 17515510 · Not cited by either guide. Concentrations are not reported by the course.

citations.title: Vitamin A antagonizes decreased cell growth and elevated collagen-degrading matrix metalloproteinases and stimulates collagen accumulation in naturally aged human skin
citations.authors: Varani J, Warner RL, Gharaee-Kermani M, et al.

note.en: human sun-protected skin by age group (n=72) plus one-week topical retinol in 53 people aged 80+ · academic · role: aged skin shows more MMPs and less collagen synthesis; one week of topical retinol lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis · PMID 10692106 · Not cited by either guide. Concentrations are not reported by the course.

citations.title: Localization, age- and site-dependent expression, and regulation of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 in skin
citations.authors: Tiganescu A, Walker EA, Hardy RS, Mayes AE, Stewart PM

note.en: human skin explants and primary dermal fibroblasts; mouse skin · academic (University of Birmingham) · role: keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts express 11β-HSD1 (not 11β-HSD2); activity rises with donor age; photo-exposed fibroblasts express more; glucocorticoid availability is regulated at a pre-receptor level, independently of systemic levels · PMID 20739946 · A&RE ch.8 ref 2; verified

citations.title: 11β-Hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase blockade prevents age-induced skin structure and function defects
citations.authors: Tiganescu A, Tahrani AA, Morgan SA, et al.

note.en: human skin biopsies (young vs older; photo-exposed vs photo-protected) + 11β-HSD1 knockout mice · academic (University of Birmingham) · role: 11β-HSD1 activity elevated in aged and photo-exposed human skin; knockout mice protected from age-induced dermal atrophy; physiological cortisol inhibits collagen biosynthesis in dermal fibroblasts · PMID 23722901 · not cited by the guides; open access PMC3696573

citations.title: Oral 11β-HSD1 inhibitor AZD4017 improves wound healing and skin integrity in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus: a pilot randomized controlled trial
citations.authors: Ajjan RA, Hensor EMA, Del Galdo F, et al.

note.en: investigator-initiated double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b pilot, n=28 adults with type 2 diabetes, 35 days · academic lead (University of Leeds); AstraZeneca co-authors · role: the only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes: primary outcome (ex vivo skin 11β-HSD1 activity) not met; exploratory smaller wound diameter; improved epidermal integrity but modestly impaired barrier function · PMID 35113805 · not cited by the guides; registered NCT03313297; the drug regimen is deliberately not reproduced (the lock excludes dosing)

citations.title: Glucocorticoids and Skin Healing in Diabetes (GC-SHealD)
citations.authors: University of Leeds (sponsor)

note.en: registered phase 2 pilot · academic · role: status: the only registered trial of an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor with skin outcomes found (ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API, 2026-09-24, terms '11beta-HSD1', '11-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 inhibitor', AZD4017, SPI-62, clofutriben); none tests skin ageing. AZD4017 has no Drugs@FDA record (openFDA drugsfda query, 2026-09-24) · CT.gov API 2026-09-24; results published as Ajjan 2022

citations.title: The diagnosis of Cushing's syndrome: an Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline
citations.authors: Nieman LK, Biller BMK, Findling JW, et al.

note.en: clinical practice guideline (GRADE) · professional society (Endocrine Society) · role: A&RE ch.8 ref 5. Table 1: features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome = easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy, striae (especially reddish-purple and >1 cm wide); common and/or less discriminatory = facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, supraclavicular fullness, weight gain, obesity, acne, hirsutism, thin skin, fatigue, insomnia. 3.1 drug history first (oral, rectal, inhaled, topical, injected; skin creams incl. bleaching agents, herbal tonics, joint or nerve injections). 3.2 test multiple and progressive features or features unusual for age. 3.3 against widespread testing. 3.5 against random serum cortisol. Abnormal result → endocrinologist. Endogenous incidence 2–3 per million per year (European population studies); commonest cause iatrogenic. · PMID 18334580 · full text read at pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (PMC2386281) 2026-09-24; test names only, doses not reproduced

citations.title: Estrogens and aging skin
citations.authors: Thornton MJ

note.en: narrative review · academic · role: A&RE ch.9 ref 2 and the single reference NAMS 2022 cites for its skin key point; quotes collagen falling 'by as much as 30% in the first five years after menopause' citing Brincat 1985 and Affinito 1999 · PMID 24194966 · open access PMC3772914, read in full 2026-09-24

citations.title: Induction of collagen by estradiol: difference between sun-protected and photodamaged human skin in vivo
citations.authors: Rittié L, Kang S, Voorhees JJ, Fisher GJ

note.en: vehicle-controlled in vivo biopsy study, n=70 (40 postmenopausal women, 30 men, mean age 75), 2 weeks · academic (University of Michigan) · role: ERα, ERβ and GPR30 expressed similarly in aged and photoaged skin; topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III and collagen I in sun-protected hip skin but not in photoaged forearm or face · PMID 18794456 · registered NCT00113100; concentrations deliberately not reproduced

citations.title: Long-term effects of the menopause and sex hormones on skin thickness
citations.authors: Brincat M, Moniz CJ, Studd JW, et al.

note.en: biopsy comparison of implant-treated vs untreated postmenopausal women · academic (London) · role: in untreated women skin collagen declined in relation to years since menopause, not chronological age · PMID 3978054 · cited by Thornton 2013 for the 30% figure; the abstract does not state it

citations.title: A study of the decrease of skin collagen content, skin thickness, and bone mass in the postmenopausal woman
citations.authors: Brincat M, Kabalan S, Studd JW, et al.

note.en: observational study of postmenopausal women · academic (London) · role: skin collagen content, skin thickness and bone mass each declined by 1–2% per year after menopause, related to years since menopause · PMID 3120067 · primary source for the per-year figure

citations.title: Effects of postmenopausal hypoestrogenism on skin collagen
citations.authors: Affinito P, Palomba S, Sorrentino C, et al.

note.en: biopsy study, n=32 (14 pre-, 18 postmenopausal) · academic (Naples) · role: type I and III collagen lower after menopause; inversely correlated with years since menopause (and with age) · PMID 10656502 · cited by Thornton 2013 for the 30% figure; the abstract does not state it

citations.title: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study on the effect of conjugated estrogens on skin thickness
citations.authors: Maheux R, Naud F, Rioux M, et al.

note.en: double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=60, 12 months · academic (Québec); sponsor not stated in abstract · role: systemic conjugated estrogens increased skin thickness (biopsy, great-trochanter skin) vs placebo · PMID 8116726 · not cited by the guides; cited by Thornton 2013

citations.title: The effects of systemic hormonal replacement therapy on the skin of postmenopausal women
citations.authors: Sauerbronn AV, Fonseca AM, Bagnoli VR, et al.

note.en: double-blind placebo-controlled RCT, n=41, 6 months · academic (São Paulo) · role: upper-arm skin collagen rose 6.49% with HT only; other skin parameters unchanged · PMID 10687834 · not cited by the guides; regimen deliberately not reproduced

citations.title: Does hormone therapy improve age-related skin changes in postmenopausal women? A randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, placebo-controlled multicenter study assessing the effects of norethindrone acetate and ethinyl estradiol in the improvement of mild to moderate age-related skin changes in postmenopausal women
citations.authors: Phillips TJ, Symons J, Menon S; HT Study Group

note.en: double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre RCT, n=485, 48 weeks, low-dose continuous combined HT · multicentre; sponsor not stated in the abstract (check funding) · role: the largest RCT of HT on facial skin: no significant difference from placebo in investigator-assessed wrinkling or sagging or self-assessed wrinkling; authors caution against extrapolating to higher doses, longer use or perimenopause · PMID 18625536 · not cited by either guide; included in Pivazyan 2023's wrinkle pooling

citations.title: Effects of hormones on skin wrinkles and rigidity vary by race/ethnicity: four-year follow-up from the ancillary skin study of the Kronos Early Estrogen Prevention Study
citations.authors: Owen CM, Pal L, Mumford SL, et al.

note.en: randomized double-blind placebo-controlled (KEEPS ancillary), women 42–58 within 36 months of last period, oral CEE or transdermal estradiol vs placebo, 4 years · independent (NICHD-funded) · role: no significant difference in total wrinkle or rigidity scores between either HT arm and placebo over 4 years; race/ethnicity was the strongest predictor · PMID 27393520 · not cited by either guide; not in Pivazyan 2023; skin-cohort size not given in the abstract

citations.title: Skin Rejuvenation in Women using Menopausal Hormone Therapy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citations.authors: Pivazyan L, Avetisyan J, Loshkareva M, Abdurakhmanova A

note.en: systematic review + meta-analysis, 15 studies (1,589 patients), RCTs and non-randomized studies · academic; no funding declared · role: pooled: elasticity SMD 0.28 (4 studies, I² 76%), thickness 1.27 (3 trials, I² 95%), collagen 2.01 (2 studies, I² 98%), wrinkles −0.30 (2 trials incl. a topical cream, I² 64%), dryness no difference; authors state MHT should not be considered an independent treatment for skin ageing; KEEPS not included · PMID 38230593 · A&RE ch.9 ref 8; open access PMC10796198, read in full 2026-09-24

citations.title: Effect of a conjugated oestrogen (Premarin) cream on ageing facial skin. A comparative study with a placebo cream
citations.authors: Creidi P, Faivre B, Agache P, et al.

note.en: randomized double-blind parallel-group, n=54 women 52–70, facial cream vs placebo cream, 24 weeks · sponsor not stated in abstract · role: topical conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles vs placebo; laxity, roughness and pigmentation no different between groups · PMID 7799828 · not cited by the guides; amount and strength deliberately not reproduced

citations.title: Topical estrogen accelerates cutaneous wound healing in aged humans associated with an altered inflammatory response
citations.authors: Ashcroft GS, Greenwell-Wild T, Horan MA, Wahl SM, Ferguson MW

note.en: randomized placebo-patch study, 18 women + 18 men (healthy, elderly), acute punch wounds · academic (NIH / Manchester) · role: topical estrogen reduced day-7 wound size and increased wound collagen and strength in both sexes · PMID 10514397 · not cited by the guides; open access PMC1867002

citations.title: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society
citations.authors: North American Menopause Society (2022 Hormone Therapy Advisory Panel)

claims.text: Human evidence on facial change during incretin-driven weight loss is observational and small: a retrospective imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial and about 7% per 10 kg lost, and a survey of 1,226 patients found self-reported sagging, facial volume loss and hair loss rising with the percentage of weight lost. summary.en: The skin as an endocrine organ; four immuno-endocrine microenvironments; local peripheral endocrine axes (HPA, thyroid, somatotropic, melanocortin); Hormone Cell Atlas cutaneous receptor distribution; endocrine senescence and SASP pathophysiology.

objective.en: By the end, you can analyze the autonomous neuro-immuno-endocrine physiology of the skin and evaluate how local steroidogenesis, receptor expression, and cellular senescence drive structural dermal aging.

title.en: The skin as an endocrine organ, and how it ages · three lessons

description.en: Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.

units.tutorContext: Module 1 teaches cutaneous neuro-immuno-endocrine physiology with every finding labelled by evidence type (mechanism, human evidence, regulatory status, open question). The skin is described as four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) that signal locally, via sensory nerves and via the circulation (mechanism reviews, D). Skin cells express CYP11A1, 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase and make cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally (cell/tissue work, D); human scalp follicles run an HPA-like loop with cortisol secretion and CRH feedback ex vivo (Ito 2005) and a GH/IGF-1 loop ex vivo (Horesh 2023); keratinocyte glucocorticoids restrain skin inflammation in mice (Phan 2021); the thyroid-like loop is mostly mouse data. Three directions: local loop; body to skin (Cushing striae, hypothyroid skin); skin to body (vitamin D3 released into the circulation, established human physiology; a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids per reviews). Refer systemic patterns promptly (violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation), per the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide. The Hormone Cell Atlas (Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026) read RNA of 379 hormone/receptor genes in ~14 million cells and nuclei from 47 tissues incl. skin; its authors call the predictions putative and hypothesis-generating: RNA is not protein, secretion or clinical effect. The guide's pearl that serum 25(OH)D falls with sunscreen use is not borne out by field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen (Neale 2019, C; high SPF untested); never advise dropping sun protection. Senescence: p16-positive cells rise with age in human epidermis and dermis (C) and track with wrinkles and perceived age (Waaijer 2016, n=178, association, C); the SASP was defined in cultured cells (D); an MMP-1 collagen-fragmentation loop is shown in aged human dermis plus culture (D), with senescent cells a plausible, unproven driver; clearing senescent cells extends healthy lifespan in mice (D); human senotherapy data are small biomarker pilots (Hickson 2019 open-label n=9, D; Chung 2019 topical rapamycin exploratory RCT, C); no randomized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes (checked Sept 2026); the guide confines senolytics to trials. Levers with human trials: daily sunscreen (Hughes 2013, n=903, B), topical tretinoin for photoageing (GRADE A), retinol in very old skin (Kafi 2007, C). Never give doses, concentrations, regimens or sourcing; adapt 'what you do next' to the learner's role (prescriber, clinical staff, advisor) without changing evidence. No CME credit is currently offered.

learningObjectives.en: Characterize local steroidogenesis and the autonomous peripheral neuroendocrine axes operating within epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, and adnexal compartments.
Differentiate between transcriptomic hormone receptor predictions and validated endocrine secretion across cutaneous cell lineages.
Assess how senescent cutaneous cell accumulation and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) impair extracellular matrix maintenance and accelerate dermal thinning.

title.en: The skin makes its own hormones.

body.en: This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.

body.en: Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.

points.en: Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Slominski & Wortsman 2000 · Zouboulis 2004 · Roosterman 2006 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–6

body.en: Epidermis, dermis, subcutis and the adnexa each hold cells that make hormones and cells that react to them, from keratinocytes and fibroblasts to fat cells and mast cells.
Signals pass between neighbouring cells, along sensory nerves, and into the blood, where they can reach distant organs.
The framework is drawn from cell, tissue and animal work. It explains how skin behaves; each finding in this module is labelled by the evidence behind it.

audioScript.en: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. Each unit holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response, such as keratinocytes, fibroblasts, sebocytes, fat cells and mast cells. Signals move three ways. Neighbouring cells talk directly, sensory nerves carry messages in and out, and some products enter the blood and reach distant organs. Keep one distinction in view for the whole module. A signal that is made and used inside the skin is a local loop. A hormone that arrives from the blood, or leaves the skin for the rest of the body, is systemic signalling. Much of what follows is mechanism, drawn from cell, tissue and animal studies, and each finding will be labelled that way.

title.en: A steroid factory with local axes.

body.en: Skin cells carry the enzymes to build steroids from cholesterol or to activate precursors arriving in the blood, and they run shortened copies of the body's central hormone axes. Each row names the evidence it rests on, because most of it comes from cells, tissue kept alive outside the body, or mice.

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2013 · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Mancino 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6

value.en: Cholesterol to cortisol, androgens and estrogens

note.en: CYP11A1 starts the chain; 11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase and aromatase activate precursors from the blood. Cell and tissue studies.
Human scalp follicles kept alive in culture. Ex vivo, human tissue.
Genetic deletion in mouse keratinocytes. Animal evidence.
Keratinocyte growth and the hair cycle. Mostly mouse models.
Human hair follicles, ex vivo.
Pigment, barrier and local immune restraint. Module 05 returns to this.

callout.en: A local axis explains biology. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide calls it foundation, not a dosing rationale.

body.en: Hormone signals in skin run in three directions. Some are made and used in the same patch of skin. Some arrive from the blood. A few leave the skin and act on the rest of the body. Knowing which one you are looking at decides whether the answer lies in the skin or in a systemic assessment.

blocks.sourceNote: Slominski 2025 · Phan 2021 · Ito 2005 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014 · Safer 2011 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5–7

note.en: Between neighbouring cells, back on the same cell, or inside it

value.en: A circulating hormone acting on skin

note.en: The skin finding can be the visible sign of a systemic disorder

prompt.en: One finding at a time: which way does the signal run?

label.en: Keratinocytes make cortisol that restrains immune cells in the same patch of skin

why.en: Local loop. Made and used where it is produced; the functional proof comes from mice that cannot make it in keratinocytes and develop skin inflammation.

label.en: UVB turns 7-dehydrocholesterol into vitamin D3, which the blood carries to liver and kidney

why.en: Skin to body. Vitamin D3 made in the skin is released into the circulation and activated elsewhere. Established human physiology.

label.en: Violaceous striae, thin skin and easy bruising in Cushing syndrome

why.en: Body to skin. Systemic cortisol excess acting on the dermis. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide lists suspected Cushing syndrome as a reason to refer promptly.

label.en: Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol, then switch off their own CRH

why.en: Local loop, with its own feedback, running with no blood supply or nerves attached. Human tissue, ex vivo.

label.en: Skin converts circulating precursors into androgens and estrogens that add to the body's supply

why.en: Skin to body. Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating sex steroids, more so in older people; the evidence is mainly biochemical.

label.en: Dry, coarse skin and myxoedema in hypothyroidism

why.en: Body to skin. Circulating thyroid hormone sets epidermal turnover and dermal matrix; the skin signs track the systemic deficit.

label.en: Scalp follicles convert testosterone to DHT, which shrinks susceptible follicles

why.en: Local loop. 5α-reductase in the pilosebaceous unit makes DHT where it acts; the guide names it the substrate of acne, androgenetic alopecia and hirsutism.

done.en: Seven placed. Three local loops, two signals the skin sends out, and two it receives.

title.en: Read the skin before the serum.

body.en: The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.

points.en: A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5 clinical pearl and referral list · Safer 2011

body.en: Thinning and bruising, coarse dry skin, new acanthosis nigricans: each points to a systemic axis before it points to a serum.
The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapid virilisation and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly.
Local loops explain how skin behaves day to day. The guide calls them foundation, never a reason to dose anyone with a hormone.

audioScript.en: Picture the consultation where a patient asks about thinning, bruising skin. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide asks you to read that skin as a window on the whole endocrine system before reaching for a serum. Sudden thinning with easy bruising suggests cortisol excess. Coarse, dry, cool skin suggests an underactive thyroid. New acanthosis nigricans points to insulin resistance. The guide lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, rapidly progressive virilisation, and signs of an endocrine tumour as reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. The local loops from the last two moments explain how skin behaves day to day. They are foundation biology, and the guide is explicit that they are no rationale for dosing anyone with a hormone. Whatever your role, a systemic pattern in the skin gets a systemic answer.

prescriber.en: When a skin pattern suggests a systemic disorder, assess or refer before any cosmetic plan, and record that you considered it. Local skin biology is no basis for prescribing a hormone for appearance.

clinical-staff.en: If you see new striae, rapid bruising, sudden hair change or signs of virilisation, record them and raise them with the prescriber before the next treatment.

advisor.en: If a client's skin change comes with new systemic symptoms, suggest they see a prescriber before trying another product. A serum cannot answer a systemic question.

body.en: One question to close lesson 1.1.

blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 1.1

prompt.en: Fictional case. A 52-year-old has new thin, easily bruised skin on her forearms, new violaceous striae and newly raised blood pressure. She has read that skin makes its own cortisol and asks whether a cream could calm it. Which reading is right?

text.en: Her skin's own cortisol explains the picture, so the answer is local.

why.en: Local skin cortisol tunes immune activity where it is made. It does not explain new striae together with new hypertension.

text.en: The combination is a systemic pattern; the guide lists it as a reason for prompt endocrine referral before any skin treatment.

why.en: Correct. Striae, bruising and new hypertension together point to possible systemic cortisol excess: a body-to-skin signal.

text.en: Local and systemic cortisol are interchangeable, so either explanation fits.

why.en: Local synthesis acts within the skin and runs its own feedback; a systemic syndrome needs a systemic assessment.

feedback.en: Decide which direction the signal runs before you decide what to treat.

title.en: A map of fourteen million cells.

body.en: The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.

points.en: RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers

blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

body.en: RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes, cell by cell, across 47 human tissues including skin.
Which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond, including unexpected sites outside the classic glands.
Whether a cell actually makes and releases the hormone, and whether that hormone does anything there.

audioScript.en: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such as RNA for the gut hormone secretin in a type of immune cell. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide uses the atlas to argue that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed signalling networks. The word plausibly matters. Everything in the atlas starts from RNA, and RNA tells you what a cell could make. Whether the cell actually makes and releases the hormone is the question the rest of this lesson answers.

title.en: Prediction, in the authors' own words.

body.en: The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.

blocks.sourceNote: Fei & Huang-Doran, Science 2026 · hormonecellatlas.org.uk About/FAQ, read 24 Sep 2026 · Liu 2016

label.en: hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell

detail.en: Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues

means.en: The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.

doesNot.en: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

body.en: Findings about skin as an endocrine organ sit on different rungs of the same ladder. Before you see the answers, decide how far up each one reaches.

blocks.sourceNote: Fei 2026 · atlas portal · Ito 2005 · Phan 2021 · Horesh 2023 · Holick 1980 · Bikle 2014

note.en: Single-cell atlases; a prediction to confirm
Human tissue kept alive in culture, or animal models
Measured in people, in the body

callout.en: Each rung needs the one below it, and advice to a patient needs the top one.

prompt.en: Tap the highest rung each finding reaches.

label.en: A skin cell type scores high as a hormone producer in a single-cell RNA atlas

why.en: Transcript. The score comes from RNA; the atlas's authors call such predictions putative until validated.

label.en: Scalp hair follicles kept alive in culture secrete cortisol and switch off their own CRH

why.en: Function in human tissue. The loop works ex vivo; whether it shapes hair growth in a living scalp is a further step.

label.en: A brochure says skin 'has receptors for' a hormone, citing an RNA atlas

why.en: Transcript. A receptor gene on a map is where the question starts, and where this brochure stops.

label.en: Mice unable to make glucocorticoids in keratinocytes develop skin inflammation

why.en: Function in animals. Strong evidence that local glucocorticoids matter in mouse skin; in people there is only an association with inflammatory skin disease.

label.en: Sunlight on human skin forms vitamin D3 that the blood carries away

why.en: Human, in vivo. Cutaneous vitamin D3 synthesis and its release into the circulation were shown in human skin and are established physiology.

done.en: Five sorted. One reaches living people; the rest are maps or mechanisms.

title.en: A map to confirm, then a trial.

body.en: Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.

points.en: A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D

blocks.sourceNote: Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 6–7 pearls · Neale 2019 · Fei 2026 · Bikle 2014

body.en: Receptors explain how a topical could act. Whether it does is a question for a human trial.
Steroid-metabolising enzymes in skin change potency, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts.
Artificial-UV experiments show sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis; field trials of daily use did not lower blood levels. High-protection products have not been trialled.

audioScript.en: Two habits follow from the atlas. The first concerns product claims. Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts once it arrives, so the response in skin can differ from what the dose predicts. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts, and the answer still needs a trial. The second habit concerns the physiology you think you know. The guide's testing pearl says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, which the biology predicts. An independent review found that in real-life field trials, daily sunscreen did not lower blood levels, although the sunscreens tested were moderate and today's high-protection products have never been trialled. Keep recommending sun protection, and treat vitamin D as its own question.

prescriber.en: When a product or protocol is justified by 'skin has receptors for it', ask for the human trial before you prescribe. Assess vitamin D on clinical grounds, and do not advise patients to drop sun protection.

clinical-staff.en: If a patient says they stopped sunscreen to raise their vitamin D, note it and pass it to the prescriber; the trials do not support stopping.

advisor.en: Describe receptor-based product claims as hypotheses unless a human trial backs them, keep sun-protection advice unchanged, and send vitamin D questions to a prescriber.

body.en: One question to close lesson 1.2.

blocks.sourceNote: Lesson 1.2

prompt.en: A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?

text.en: That the serum reaches those fibroblasts and improves the skin.

why.en: That needs penetration data and a clinical trial; an RNA map provides neither.

text.en: That skin secretes the hormone and needs it replaced when levels fall.

why.en: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.

text.en: That fibroblasts may respond to the hormone: a hypothesis to confirm at the protein, function and clinical level.

why.en: Correct. The atlas's authors call such predictions putative and hypothesis-generating.

feedback.en: A receptor on the map is where the question starts.

title.en: Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.

body.en: A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.

points.en: Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age

blocks.sourceNote: Coppé 2008 · Ressler 2006 · Ho & Dreesen 2021 · Wang & Dreesen 2018 · Haykal 2026 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 7

body.en: A damaged cell stops dividing for good, which guards against cancer and helps wound repair.
It stays active and releases inflammatory cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors, first catalogued in cultured human cells.

title.en: What we see in human skin

body.en: Older skin holds more cells carrying the marker p16 in epidermis and dermis. No single marker is definitive.

audioScript.en: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin six and eight, enzymes that break down matrix, and growth factors. This secretory profile, the SASP, was characterised in human cells grown in the laboratory after DNA damage. In living human skin, the evidence is observational. Skin samples from older people contain more cells carrying the senescence marker p16, in both the epidermis and the dermis, and fibroblasts, keratinocytes and melanocytes can all become senescent. Researchers also caution that no single marker identifies a senescent cell with certainty, so counts depend on the marker chosen.

body.en: In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.

blocks.sourceNote: Waaijer 2016 (Leiden Longevity Study) · Ressler 2006

label.en: younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age

detail.en: Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies

means.en: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.

doesNot.en: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.

body.en: Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.

blocks.sourceNote: Shuster 1975 · Varani 2006 · Fisher 2009 · Waaijer 2016 · Baker 2016 · Xu 2018 · Hickson 2019 · Chung 2019

note.en: Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.

Small pilots measuring tissue markers. One exploratory randomized trial of topical rapamycin (36 enrolled, 19 dropped out) lowered skin p16, and clinical change was only described. No adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found (September 2026).

callout.en: A mouse lifespan result is not a skin treatment.

title.en: The levers with trials behind them.

body.en: Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.

points.en: Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)
Topical retinoids for photoageing: GRADE A
Senolytics for skin: no clinical-outcome trials yet

blocks.sourceNote: Hughes 2013 · Sitohang 2022 · Kafi 2007 · Varani 2000 · Fisher 2002 · Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology, ch. 5

body.en: A publicly funded Australian trial of 903 adults: daily sunscreen meant about a quarter less skin ageing over four and a half years.
Consistent randomized trials for tretinoin in photoaged skin; the guide's GRADE A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in very old skin.
Biomarker pilots only, so far. They sit below the levers that already have outcome data.

audioScript.en: Set the senescence story beside the interventions that have been tested in people. In Nambour, Australia, a publicly funded trial randomised 903 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen, and over four and a half years skin ageing was about a quarter lower with daily use. Topical tretinoin has a run of randomised trials in photoaged skin that agree with one another, and the Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, grade A. Retinol has smaller trials, including one in residents in their late eighties whose fine wrinkling improved and whose biopsies showed more procollagen. Both levers protect or rebuild the dermal matrix that ultraviolet light and, it is thought, the SASP erode, and both have human outcome data. Senolytics for skin have no such data yet. Keep that order in mind when a patient asks what actually works.

points.en: Senescent cells in human skin: real, and linked with visible ageing
Clearing them: mouse evidence and small human biomarker pilots
Sunscreen and retinoids: randomized human trials

why.en: Right. It keeps the registers apart and moves her toward the levers with human outcome data. The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

why.en: Senescent cells are measurable in human skin and track with wrinkles and perceived age. The biology is real; the treatment evidence is what is missing.

audioScript.en: Consider a fifty-eight-year-old patient, fictional and built from this lesson's evidence. She has read that senolytic supplements clear so-called zombie cells and reverse skin ageing, and she asks whether to start one she found online. She does not wear sunscreen every day. Three facts frame the conversation. Senescent cells really do accumulate in human skin, and their number tracks with wrinkles and with how old a person looks. The evidence that clearing them helps comes from mice, and the human studies so far are small pilots measuring markers in tissue. Daily sunscreen and topical retinoids, by contrast, have randomised trials with visible skin outcomes. The Aesthetic and Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises keeping senolytics within clinical trials. Decide what you say first.

prescriber.en: You weigh a prescription retinoid against her skin and history, document the discussion, and explain that senolytics are still at the pilot-study stage and belong in trials.

clinical-staff.en: You record what she plans to buy and anything she already takes, share the evidence summary, and pass the retinoid question to the prescriber.

advisor.en: You explain the difference between mouse and human evidence, reinforce daily sunscreen, and suggest a prescriber for a retinoid or if she wants to explore a trial.
